title: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “Quantum Phenomena” (from p. 537), p. 538. Scope: network models of the universe and quantum phenomena

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-26: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.43

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Individual quantum phenomena can be sought computationally and compared with existing experiments. The unrestricted prediction that these programs will ultimately reproduce many or all features is too vague and broad for full resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For specified causal-invariant network models, derive quantitative counterparts of superposition, interference, entanglement, measurement statistics, and unitary evolution, then compare with benchmark quantum experiments. Failure on any claimed key feature refutes that model; joint quantitative agreement would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The model class and 'key features' are open-ended.

Qualitative resemblance has weak discriminating power.

Selected quantum predictions do not establish equivalence to quantum theory.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.38
data existence: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.42
analysis feasibility: 0.35
data adequacy: 0.3

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Quantum phenomena are abundantly measured, and network programs are public, but the claim is that those programs will reproduce quantum theory. No existing dataset or finished derivation shows that they do, and the phrase 'key features' is loose enough that scattered resemblances would not decide it. A pre-registered match remains to be produced.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: List a fixed set of quantum-theory features, such as amplitudes, interference, measurement outcomes, and identical-particle statistics, and test whether a causally invariant network model reproduces them without putting in the quantum formalism. Reproduction of the pre-registered list would support the claim; failure on a core feature after the model is fixed would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Building realistic models of quantum experiments inside these programs is a large unfinished computation.

'Many if not all key features' does not name the checklist, so partial successes can always be counted as enough.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.24
discriminating power: 0.28
operationalizability: 0.36
data adequacy: 0.2
data existence: 0.34
